fields.evidence: Body: "We created a set of 10 instructions, shown in Table 3, to be encoded with job descriptions according to templates specific to each model. We used ChatGPT in this procedure to develop alternatives for the phrases 'job description' and 'resume.'" Table 3 caption: "Instructions appended to each job description before embedding generation." Example rows printed in full, e.g. ID 1 "Given a job description, retrieve resumes that satisfy the requirements"; ID 10 "Given a job description, retrieve work histories that fulfill the criteria". CAVEAT (what is missing): the actual serialized prompt string is not shown, because footnote 5 defers the wrapper to external docs: "The text formatting used to encode instructions and query texts varies between MTEs. For each model, we followed the recommended structure as described in that model's documentation for these experiments." So the instruction text is exact; the full encoded query template per model is not reproducible from the paper alone.

"We created a set of 10 instructions, shown in Table 3, to be encoded with job descriptions according to templates specific to each model." Confirmed by counting Table 3, which lists IDs 1-10. Equation (2) also sums t=1..10.

The paper averages cosine similarity over all 10 wordings BEFORE any bias test: "Cosine similarity scores were averaged over task instructions, so the updated similarity computation is as in Equation (2), where t corresponds to the index of the task instructions in Table 3 used to form job description embeddings." Equation (2): sim(r,d) = (1/10) * sum_{t=1..10} <v_r, v_dt>. Every chi-square bias test is then run on that averaged score. I checked the claim "For completeness, results for individual task instructions are also provided in the Appendix" against the actual appendix: the ONLY per-instruction figure is Figure 14 (p.20, "Appendix: Detailed Instructions Results"), and its caption is "For every model and task instruction corresponding to those in Table 3, resumes which belong to the same occupation category as a given job description (match) have significantly higher cosine similarities than those which belong to different occupation categories (unmatch) (p<0.0001)" — that is the retrieval-VALIDITY check, not a demographic effect. Figures 15-23 break results out by model and occupation, never by instruction. So no demographic effect is separately estimated under any individual wording: n = 1.

Searched and absent. grep -ic over the full text returned 0 for: 'standard deviation', ' SD ', 'variance', 'across instructions', 'across task'; 'spread' returns 1 hit and 'range of' 3 hits, all unrelated (occupational range, document-length range, range of social groups). No SD, range, min/max, error bar or between-wording variability statistic is given for any demographic effect. The per-instruction appendix figure (Figure 14) covers only match-vs-unmatch retrieval validity and reports no dispersion statistic. Because the 10 wordings are averaged inside Equation (2) before testing, the design cannot yield a between-wording dispersion for the headline effect.

No condition differs from another by whitespace or punctuation only. I read all 10 rows of Table 3: every pair differs by at least one content word, drawn from three synonym slots — {job description | job posting | job profile}, {resumes | work histories | employment records}, {satisfy the requirements | meet the specifications | fulfill the criteria}. The closest pair is ID 1 "Given a job description, retrieve resumes that satisfy the requirements" vs ID 8 "Given a job posting, retrieve resumes that satisfy the requirements" — a lexical substitution, not a null edit. grep -ic returned 0 for 'whitespace', 'punctuat', 'control condition', 'ablation'; 'formatting' returns 2 hits, both about model-specific encoding templates (footnote 5) and the cited Sclar et al. 2023 prompt-formatting paper, not a controlled null-edit arm. A null-edit control was possible under this design and is simply absent.

fields.evidence: What IS there — a full name-subset swap: "When names which had approximately equivalent frequencies in the DOLMA corpus were used, we find that resumes with Black names are preferred to those with White names in 51.9% of 27 tests, while those with White names are preferred to those with Black names in only 22.2% of tests. This is the reverse pattern than what is observed when names are selected based on population proportional frequencies." Results are also broken out by model (3) and occupation (9) in Figures 4-9 and 15-23. What is MISSING: no selection rate, chi-square contribution, or effect estimate is reported for any individual name. Tables 4-6 give per-name DOLMA frequency and distinctiveness score only — inputs, not outcomes. grep -ic returned 0 for 'sensitivity analysis', 'robustness', 'ablation'. With 20 names per cell there is no way from the paper to tell whether an effect is carried by one or two names.

Tokenization of the manipulated names is never discussed or controlled. grep -i over the full text and over an independent PyMuPDF extraction of all 25 PDF pages returned 0 hits for 'tokeniz', 'subword', 'BPE'. The 8 'token' hits are all unrelated: next-token prediction as a training objective (x2), generation cost of new tokens, DOLMA's 3.1 trillion tokens (x2), the 1,300-token document truncation, and 'Average length is 1,154 tokens' in Figure 12. ADJACENT BUT DIFFERENT: names are matched on log corpus frequency in DOLMA via infini-gram ("Corpus frequencies were determined using infini-gram (Liu et al. 2024)... and the DOLMA corpus"), and on a distinctiveness score. Corpus-frequency matching is not token-length or token-boundary matching, and the paper never states how many tokens the substituted first names occupy or whether that varies by group.

No batch size, padding strategy, or parallelism is stated. This is a live concern here rather than a formality, because padding and batch composition can perturb the last-hidden-state embeddings that the entire measurement is built on.

The study performs a single forward pass per document to extract an embedding — "Document embeddings were extracted from the last hidden state of a model and normalized before computing their cosine similarity" — with no autoregressive generation anywhere in the measurement pipeline, so KV-cache reuse across decoding steps and prompt-cache reuse across turns cannot affect any reported quantity. Recording the negative search for completeness: grep -ic returned 0 for 'cache', 'caching', and 'prompt cach' across the full text, and a regex count over the whole PDF also returned 0 for 'cache'. (The paper does implicitly reuse each resume embedding across all 571 job descriptions, since similarity is a dot product of separately computed vectors, but it never frames or states this as a caching policy.)

No text is generated in the measured pipeline. The outcome is cosine similarity between embeddings — "sim(r, d) = <v_r, v_d>" and Equation (2) — so temperature, top-p, seed and greedy-vs-sampled have no operative meaning for the audit itself. No repeated measurement of an identical input is described, and no run-to-run agreement statistic is given. grep -ic returned 0 for ' runs', 'trial', 'stability', 'replicat' as re-running (the 3 'replicat' hits are substantive — 'replicating real-world patterns of bias', 'replicating the distribution of names', 'replicate existing societal patterns'). The 10 task instructions give 10 measurements per resume-JD pair, but under different wordings and they are averaged, not compared for agreement. The paper never asserts that its embedding extraction is deterministic.

The paper uses no bootstrap and reports no confidence intervals, so there is no resampling unit to state. Negative searches: grep -ic returned 0 for 'bootstrap', 'confidence interval', '95%', 'resampl', 'permutation'; a whole-PDF regex count for 'bootstrap' was also 0. Inference is entirely chi-square on counts: "A chi-square test is then used to determine whether the most similar resumes are distributed equally amongst relevant groups". The unit of observation for that test IS stated: "Chi-square tests require a minimum of five observed values for valid population estimates (Franke, Ho, and Christie 2012); our dataset far exceeds that, with at least 160 resume documents for every bias test", and "At this threshold, a minimum of 160 resumes were selected for each job description, and a total of 27 bias tests were conducted" — note these two sentences state the >=160 floor as per-test and per-job-description respectively, which is an internal inconsistency in the paper. Non-independence (the same 554 base resumes reappear under 40 names and are scored against 571 job descriptions) is never addressed in the test's error model.

Searched and absent. grep -ic returned 0 for 'Bonferroni', 'false discovery', 'FDR', 'Benjamini', 'multiple comparison', 'alpha', 'significance level'; a whole-PDF regex count for 'correction' was also 0. The count of significant tests IS the headline statistic, which makes the absence of any family-wise or FDR adjustment load-bearing rather than incidental.

"After this, the dataset contained 554 resumes and 571 job descriptions across nine occupations (Chief Executive, Marketing and Sales Manager, Miscellaneous Manager, Human Resources Worker, Accountant and Auditor, Miscellaneous Engineer, Secondary School Teacher, Designer, and Miscellaneous Sales and Related Worker)." Table 1 caption: "Resume screening was investigated for nine occupations." Consistent with the 27 = 3 models x 9 occupations test count. Results, verbatim: "In 85.1% of 27 tests for racial bias in resume screening, White names were preferred, and only in 8.6% of tests were Black names preferred"; "In 51.9% of 27 tests for gender bias in resume screening, male names were preferred to female names, and only in 11.1% of tests were female names preferred"; "White male names are significantly preferred in all 27 tests (p<0.05)." negative_check:
**All seven absences confirmed in the paper itself.** Verified independently: full text (`lit/text/wilson_caliskan_2024_aies.txt`, 2,010 lines, read end to end), an independent PyMuPDF extraction of all 25 PDF pages, a de-hyphenated normalization of that extraction (to catch line-broken words like `quan-\ntization` — the reader's raw greps would have missed these; re-ran and still 0), and **visual rendering of the figure pages**, which is necessary because the figures are vector drawings whose axis/legend text is NOT in the PDF text layer (page 20 extracts only 338 chars). Inspected pages 6, 7, 15, 19, 20, 21 as images: Figures 4/10/11 show per-model lines with a gray non-significance band (no error bars, no SD); Figure 14 shows per-instruction violins of match-vs-unmatch cosine similarity only, with no demographic contrast and no numeric dispersion statistic; Figures 12/13 are document-length histograms. Table 3 (lines 1124–1133) verified: all 10 instructions differ by content words; closest pair is ID 1 vs ID 8 (`job description` → `job posting`), a lexical substitution, not a null edit.

**However — three of these ARE documented in the paper's own released code repository**, which the paper cites in-text ("The code and data produced by this research are available at https://github.com/kyrawilson/Resume-Screening-Bias"). The reader explicitly declined to check it. If your matrix scopes "reported" to the paper PDF, the negatives stand; if it scopes to the study's released artifacts, three cells flip:

- **quantization_reported** — `embeddings.py`: `AutoModel.from_pretrained(args['model'], device_map='auto', torch_dtype=torch.float16)`; GritLM loaded with `torch_dtype="auto"`; embeddings cast via `torch.as_tensor(q_rep, dtype=torch.float16)`. fp16 throughout, never stated in the paper.
- **serving_stack** — `README.md`: `-m, --model  Name of HuggingFace model to use  default='intfloat/e5-mistral-7b-instruct'`. `environment.yml`: PyTorch 2.2.0 + CUDA 12.1, transformers 4.39.3, sentence-transformers 2.6.1, accelerate 0.27.2, MTEB 1.5.2, Python 3.12.1; env path `/gscratch/stf/kywi/envs/LLMtest` (UW cluster). Loading is `AutoModel.from_pretrained(..., device_map='auto')`.
- **concurrency_or_batching** — `README.md`: `-b, --batch_size  Batch size  default=1`. `embeddings.py` tokenizes with `padding=False, truncation=True` then `tokenizer.pad(batch_dict, padding=True, return_attention_mask=True, return_tensors='pt')`, and iterates one item at a time. This directly addresses the reader's stated concern about padding perturbing last-hidden-state embeddings — the default is batch size 1.

Also relevant: `-l, --max_length  Max number of tokens to embed  default=4096` (paper uses 1,300, matching the text).

**Still absent in both paper and repo**: `dispersion_across_wordings`, `null_edit_control`, `token_matching` (no tokenizer-level name analysis anywhere), `n_repeats` (no random seed set in `embeddings.py`; no re-run agreement statistic), `multiplicity_correction` (no correction in README or paper; every threshold uncorrected).

One clarification on the reader's `dispersion_across_wordings` evidence: Figure 14 does display distributional spread (violins) per instruction, but across resume–job-description pairs within an instruction, for the retrieval-validity outcome only — not between-wording variability of any demographic effect. The reader's conclusion is right; the phrasing "reports no dispersion statistic" is accurate for a summary statistic but slightly understates that the figure is a distributional plot.
